name.text: Functions in Real Life — domain restrictions from context (discrete vs continuous)

questiontext.text:
A ticket vendor at a school sports day sells tickets for KSh {@price@} each. If \(n\) tickets are sold, the total revenue in shillings is

\[ R(n) = {@price*n@}. \]

Which of the following best describes the domain of \(R\) in this real-life context?

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

generalfeedback.text:
The formula \(R(n) = {@price*n@}\) can be evaluated for every real number \(n\), so its algebraic domain is all real numbers. But the context restricts which inputs make sense. You can only sell a whole number of tickets, and you cannot sell a negative number of them. So the realistic domain is \(n \in \{0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots\}\), the non-negative whole numbers. The function is discrete, not continuous: its graph is a set of separate points, not a line.

Always check whether the real-world context restricts the domain beyond what the algebra alone allows.

questiondescription.text: Grade 11 Functions 16.11 (Functions in Real Life). Tests recognising that a real-world context (selling whole tickets) restricts the domain beyond what the bare algebraic formula would allow, contrasting the algebraic domain with the realistic domain. The price is randomised only cosmetically; the answer does not depend on it.

falsefeedback.text: Think about which values of \(n\) make sense when selling tickets. Can you sell half a ticket? Can you sell a negative number of tickets?
